messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries—Chūnjié (Spring Festival) is all about warmth and good intentions, and your cousins will appreciate any effort you make! Here are a few thoughtful ways to handle the hongbao (red envelope) situation last-minute: 1. **Quick DIY Hongbao** If you can’t buy ready-made ones, make your own! Use red paper or cardstock, fold it into an envelope shape, and add some festive decorations (gold pens, stickers, or even calligraphy-style writing). A handmade touch can actually make it more personal and memorable. 2. **Digital Hongbao (if appropriate)** If your cousins are tech-savvy or live far away, consider sending a digital hongbao via WeChat (if you're in China or connected to family there). It’s fast, convenient, and still carries the festive spirit. Just add a warm message! 3. **Buy in Bulk (Last-Minute Run)** Head to a local Asian grocery store, convenience store, or mall—they often stock hongbao during the Lunar New Year season. Even last-minute, you should be able to find some. Pick a simple but elegant design to keep it classy. 4. **Pair with a Small Gift** If you’re really short on time or funds, pair a smaller hongbao (even with a symbolic amount like ¥8 or $8 for good luck) with a small gift—like mandarins, candy, or a cute Lunar New Year trinket. It shows extra thought. 5. **Be Honest and Warm** When handing it over, a simple, “Sorry I was running late this year, but I didn’t want to miss giving you your blessing!” goes a long way. Your cousins will care more about the gesture than perfection. 6. **Set a Reminder for Next Year!** Jot it down in your calendar now—maybe even schedule a hongbao shopping date a month before Chūnjié next time. Future you will thank you. Remember: The hongbao symbolizes good wishes and blessings. As long as your heart is in the right place, your cousins will feel the love. Xīnnián kuàilè! 🧧🎉

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: 1 It’s not wrong to stop making dinner every night when your husband isn’t home to eat it. Relationships involve mutual care and practicality. If he’s consistently working late and choosing to eat out, adjusting your routine is reasonable and self-aware. It shows respect for your own time and energy, and it adapts to real-life circumstances. What matters most is communication and ensuring both partners feel cared for in ways that work for them—whether that’s through home-cooked meals, quality time, or other acts of love. Continuing to cook daily when it’s no longer needed could lead to burnout or resentment, which isn’t healthy for either of you.
